sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
**Everything needed to study the course is inside this notebook:** twenty detailed chapters, three worked examples per chapter, inline runnable local examples, the complete custom SQLite saver, and PostgreSQL/MongoDB/Redis implementation recipes.

Read the Markdown explanations and code together. Run executable cells from top to bottom after installing the packages below. The code does not import companion `labs.py` files. Local examples need no API keys and use temporary databases. Database-server examples are disabled until you explicitly enable them and provide your connection variables.

The verified package baseline is Python 3.12 / LangGraph 1.2.18. [Supporting guide](checkpointers_masterclass/README.md) · [Validation details](checkpointers_masterclass/VALIDATION.md) · [Sources](checkpointers_masterclass/SOURCES.md).

sections.title: Shared imports and the first reusable graph
sections.body: This setup defines a tiny graph that increments `count` and a helper that constructs a thread config. Their implementations are visible here and reused by later cells. ```python from __future__ import annotations import argparse import asyncio import operator import sqlite3 from contextlib import closing from pathlib import Path from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory from typing import Annotated from typing_extensions import TypedDict from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, HumanMessage, RemoveMessage from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite.aio import AsyncSqliteSaver from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END, MessagesState from langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore from langgraph.types import Command, RetryPolicy, interrupt import json import os from uuid import uuid4 import importlib.metadata as package_metadata print("LangGraph:", package_metadata.version("langgraph")) class CounterState(TypedDict): count: int def counter_graph(saver): builder = StateGraph(CounterState) builder.add_node("increment", lambda s: {"count": s["count"] + 1}) builder.add_edge(START, "increment") builder.add_edge("increment", END) return builder.compile(checkpointer=saver) def config(thread="example", **kwargs): return {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread, **kwargs}} ```

sections.title: Build the correct vocabulary
sections.body:
**State** is the data flowing through your graph: messages, an order number, a
retrieved document ID, or a running total. A node normally returns an update to
state. A **reducer** determines how that update combines with the previous value.

A **checkpointer** is the storage implementation passed to `compile`. A
**checkpoint** is an internal persisted execution record. A **StateSnapshot** is
the public object returned by `get_state` or `get_state_history`. These terms are
related, but saving `snapshot.values` alone does not implement a saver.

| Object | Important content | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| User state | Application fields | Nodes read and update these values |
| Internal checkpoint | ID, timestamp, channel values, versions, versions seen | Runtime reconstructs progress and scheduling |
| Checkpoint tuple | Checkpoint, metadata, config, parent config, pending writes | Saver returns all associated persistence information |
| Public StateSnapshot | `values`, `next`, `config`, `metadata`, `created_at`, `parent_config`, `tasks` | Application inspects progress without decoding database blobs |

`channel_versions` tell the runtime which channel value is newer.
`versions_seen` tracks which versions a node has already observed. They are not
your business object's schema version. Runtime channels may include keys you did
not declare in your state class. Preserve the complete runtime checkpoint rather
than selecting only familiar fields.

A **super-step** groups the nodes scheduled for one execution round. Parallel
nodes can share a round. Their individual writes and the completed round's
checkpoint serve different purposes. See the [official checkpoint guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers).

diagrams.title: Checkpointers: a saved snapshot after every super-step
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  I["invoke - thread_id=user-42"] --> N1["node A"] --> C1[("checkpoint 1")]
  C1 --> N2["node B"] --> C2[("checkpoint 2")]
  C2 --> N3["node C"] --> C3[("checkpoint 3 - latest")]
  C3 -. "next invoke, same thread_id" .-> R["resume with full history"]
  C1 -. "time travel - checkpoint_id" .-> F["fork from an old state"]
diagrams.explain: Compile a graph with a **checkpointer** (MemorySaver, SqliteSaver, PostgresSaver…) and every super-step writes a snapshot keyed by `thread_id`. Invoking again with the same thread continues the conversation; a different thread starts fresh. Old checkpoints enable **time travel** — replay or fork from any earlier state — and they are what makes human-in-the-loop interrupts possible.

sections.title: Example 1 — A counter reveals the actual saved timeline
sections.body:
**Scenario:** persist one arithmetic operation before introducing an LLM.

```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
from common import counter_graph, config

saver = InMemorySaver()
graph = counter_graph(saver)
c = config("counter-1")
result = graph.invoke({"count": 10}, c)
for snapshot in reversed(list(graph.get_state_history(c))):
    print(snapshot.metadata["step"], snapshot.values, snapshot.next)
```

In the pinned local lab this prints the progression:

```text
-1 {}              ('__start__',)
 0 {'count': 10}   ('increment',)
 1 {'count': 11}   ()
```

The input is accepted before `increment` executes. The completed result has an
empty `next` tuple. The first internal input checkpoint does not yet expose the
input as ordinary state. Therefore “one node means one database row” is the wrong
assumption. More complicated graphs create additional checkpoints and task writes.

**Try it:** add a second node that doubles the count. Inspect the checkpoint where
`next == ('double',)`. Its values should already include the first node's update.

sections.title: Example 2 — New input is different from continuing saved work
sections.body:
**Scenario:** the counter has finished at 11.

```python
assert graph.invoke(None, c)["count"] == 11
assert graph.invoke({"count": 20}, c)["count"] == 21
```

`None` asks the runtime to continue from saved execution state. There is no work
left in the completed counter, so it returns 11. A dictionary submits a fresh
input to this thread. The ordinary `count` field is replaced by 20, and the
increment node produces 21. A conversation's message reducer behaves differently
because it merges messages instead of replacing a scalar.

**Use this distinction:** resume a failed workflow with `None`; submit the next
chat message as a new input dictionary; resume a dynamic human interrupt with
`Command(resume=...)`. These calls are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Example 3 — Saver lifetime explains apparently missing memory
sections.body: **Scenario:** you compile a graph inside every HTTP request. ```python same_storage_graph = counter_graph(saver) assert same_storage_graph.get_state(c).values["count"] == 21 new_storage_graph = counter_graph(InMemorySaver()) assert new_storage_graph.get_state(c).values == {} ``` Recompilation is not itself the cause of data loss. The second graph uses a fresh, empty RAM saver. A file/database-backed saver can reconstruct state after both the original graph object and the original process are gone. With RAM, you must keep the same saver object alive, and even then a process restart loses it. **Run all three:** `python labs.py foundations`. ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python def foundations(): # 1. A linear graph has input/loop checkpoints, not just the final answer. saver = InMemorySaver() graph = counter_graph(saver) c = config("foundations") assert graph.invoke({"count": 10}, c)["count"] == 11 history = list(graph.get_state_history(c)) assert len(history) >= 3 assert history[0].values == {"count": 11} print("1. History:", [(s.metadata["step"], s.values, s.next) for s in history]) # 2. A completed checkpoint has no remaining work. None is not a new input. assert graph.invoke(None, c)["count"] == 11 assert graph.invoke({"count": 20}, c)["count"] == 21 print("2. None resumes; a dict submits a new input.") # 3. Recreating the saver loses RAM history; reusing it preserves history. assert counter_graph(saver).get_state(c).values["count"] == 21 assert counter_graph(InMemorySaver()).get_state(c).values == {} print("3. Saver lifetime determines RAM lifetime.") ``` ```python foundations() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
The storage address is conceptually `(thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id)`.
The application chooses the thread, the runtime commonly chooses namespaces for
subgraphs, and checkpoint creation generates checkpoint IDs.

| Identifier | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `thread_id` | `tenant-a:chat-17` | A conversation or workflow instance |
| `checkpoint_ns` | Empty string at root | A graph/subgraph checkpoint namespace |
| `checkpoint_id` | Runtime-generated ordered identifier | A particular historical point |
| User ID | `user-42` | Your authenticated application identity |
| Request/run ID | `request-900` | One invocation; a thread may have many |

Neither a thread ID nor a namespace authenticates the caller. Your application
must resolve an authorized conversation before calling graph APIs. Do not let a
client change `thread_id` to inspect somebody else's history.

sections.title: Example 1 — One user, two conversations
sections.body:
The runnable `identity` lab stores count 2 in `tenant-a:chat-1` and count 101 in
`tenant-a:chat-2`, using one saver. Reading chat 1 still returns 2.

```python
graph.invoke({"count": 1}, config("tenant-a:chat-1"))
graph.invoke({"count": 100}, config("tenant-a:chat-2"))
```

If you used only `user-42` as the thread ID for both chats, the chats would share
one state history. If you generated a new UUID on every message, each message
would start a separate conversation. Generate the conversation ID once, save it
in your application, and reuse it for subsequent turns.

For a one-time document extraction job, use a separate thread for each job. The
same user may own thousands of job threads without mixing their state.

sections.title: Example 2 — Latest state versus an explicit historical state
sections.body:
```python
c = config("tenant-a:chat-1")
old = graph.get_state(c)
graph.invoke({"count": 10}, c)
assert graph.get_state(c).values["count"] == 11
assert graph.get_state(old.config).values["count"] == 2
```

The thread-only config asks for the latest record. `old.config` contains an
explicit checkpoint ID, so it addresses the earlier record. Preserve the full
config returned by snapshot APIs when you want an exact replay/fork point.

A branch does not automatically become a new thread. Several branches can live
in one thread history. Your UI may need to retain the selected branch's explicit
config rather than treating “latest” as a business-approved branch.

sections.title: Example 3 — Namespaces separate parent and child execution records
sections.body: The storage-level lab writes the same checkpoint into a second namespace, `worker-demo`. A lookup in `missing` returns nothing. This proves that the namespace is part of the lookup identity; it does not demonstrate invoking a top-level graph with an invented subgraph path. In real graph composition, let LangGraph create child namespaces. The `composition` lab produces a root namespace and a generated `child:...` namespace. Use `graph.get_state(config, subgraphs=True)` to inspect supported child state and follow the returned configs. Do not guess generated task IDs. There are also three different meanings of “namespace” in this course: 1. A PostgreSQL schema groups database tables. 2. A checkpoint namespace separates graph execution contexts. 3. A Store namespace groups application key/value memories. Choosing one does not configure the others. **Run:** `python labs.py identity`. For actual child graphs, see chapter 14. ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python def identity(): saver = InMemorySaver() graph = counter_graph(saver) # 1. Different conversations remain separate with one shared saver. graph.invoke({"count": 1}, config("tenant-a:chat-1")) graph.invoke({"count": 100}, config("tenant-a:chat-2")) assert graph.get_state(config("tenant-a:chat-1")).values["count"] == 2 print("1. Two conversation IDs preserve separate histories.") # 2. Explicit checkpoint ID selects an old immutable point. c = config("tenant-a:chat-1") old = graph.get_state(c) graph.invoke({"count": 10}, c) assert graph.get_state(old.config).values["count"] == 2 assert graph.get_state(c).values["count"] == 11 print("2. Explicit checkpoint ID reads the old value 2.") # 3. Storage-level namespace isolation; use generated subgraph namespaces # in real graph runs, not arbitrary namespace strings at top-level invoke. original = saver.get_tuple(old.config) saver.put(config("tenant-a:chat-1", checkpoint_ns="worker-demo"), original.checkpoint, original.metadata, {}) assert saver.get_tuple(config("tenant-a:chat-1", checkpoint_ns="worker-demo")) assert saver.get_tuple(config("tenant-a:chat-1", checkpoint_ns="missing")) is None print("3. Saver keys include the namespace; this is not authorization.") ``` ```python identity() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
A checkpointer persists the state produced by your graph. It does not decide
whether lists should append, messages should replace, or counters should add.
Those behaviors come from state channels and reducers.

`MessagesState` gives the `messages` field message-aware merging through
`add_messages`. An ordinary scalar field typically keeps the last update. An
`Annotated[list[str], operator.add]` field concatenates list updates; it does not
deduplicate them. The lab uses these three shapes in different places so you can
observe their consequences.

sections.title: Example 1 — Accumulate two turns without sending the old transcript again
sections.body:
The `messages` lab uses a deterministic reply function that counts user messages.

```python
graph.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(content="Hello", id="u1")]}, c)
out = graph.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(content="Again", id="u2")]}, c)
```

The first invocation saves one human and one assistant message. The second
invocation adds one human and one assistant message, giving four messages. The
reply says `Received 2 user turns.` It can count both because the old state is
loaded before the reply node runs.

Send only new messages unless you deliberately need to reconcile a complete
transcript. Resending old messages with new IDs appends duplicates. This is a
reducer/identity issue, not a database corruption issue.

sections.title: Example 2 — Correct a message by preserving its ID
sections.body:
```python
graph.update_state(c, {
    "messages": [HumanMessage(content="Corrected hello", id="u1")]
})
```

The first human message changes, and the message count stays four. The reducer
recognizes the same ID and replaces that message. A new ID would create another
message. `update_state` creates another checkpoint; it does not modify all the
older stored versions of `u1`.

Suppose a human reviewer corrects an extracted customer name. For a scalar
`customer_name`, an update replaces the field directly. For a list reducer that
adds values, supplying the full corrected list might append to the old list.
Always inspect the field's reducer before editing saved state.

sections.title: Example 3 — Remove a current message and understand historical retention
sections.body: ```python before = graph.get_state(c).config graph.update_state(c, {"messages": [RemoveMessage(id="u2")]}) ``` The latest state has three messages. Reading `before` still yields four. This is useful for debugging, but it means current-state deletion is not complete data erasure. A retention/deletion operation must address older checkpoints, pending writes, Store items, exports and backups according to your application's policy. Message trimming or summarization similarly reduces future context; it does not erase earlier checkpoints. When working with tool calls, preserve valid assistant-tool message relationships. Removing one side alone can leave a transcript that a model provider rejects. **Run:** `python labs.py messages`. The three assertions verify append, replacement, and current-versus-historical deletion. LangChain's agent memory uses this graph state mechanism; see [short-term memory](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/short-term-memory). ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python def messages(): def reply(state): humans = [m for m in state["messages"] if m.type == "human"] return {"messages": [AIMessage(content=f"Received {len(humans)} user turns.")]} graph = StateGraph(MessagesState).add_node("reply", reply).add_edge( START, "reply").add_edge("reply", END).compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) c = config("messages") # 1. Submit only the new message. add_messages merges it with saved history. graph.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(content="Hello", id="u1")]}, c) out = graph.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(content="Again", id="u2")]}, c) assert len(out["messages"]) == 4 print("1.", out["messages"][-1].content) # 2. Same message ID replaces that message, rather than duplicating it. graph.update_state(c, {"messages": [HumanMessage(content="Corrected hello", id="u1")]}) state = graph.get_state(c) assert len(state.values["messages"]) == 4 assert state.values["messages"][0].content == "Corrected hello" print("2. Replaced u1; message count is still 4.") # 3. Deletion changes current state, but old checkpoints still contain u2. before = state.config graph.update_state(c, {"messages": [RemoveMessage(id="u2")]}) assert len(graph.get_state(c).values["messages"]) == 3 assert len(graph.get_state(before).values["messages"]) == 4 print("3. RemoveMessage changes current state; historical data remains.") ``` ```python messages() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Use a two-node pricing graph: `price` writes base 100; `tax` adds 10%, producing
110. This makes the difference between reading history and executing history
visible without a model or external API.

sections.title: Example 1 — Inspect the checkpoint immediately before tax
sections.body:
```python
history = list(graph.get_state_history(c))
before_tax = next(s for s in history if s.next == ("tax",))
print(before_tax.values)  # {'base': 100}
print(before_tax.next)    # ('tax',)
```

History is returned newest first by the savers used here. Select a checkpoint by
its meaning, such as `next`, rather than assuming `history[2]` always represents
the desired point. Changing the graph can change how many checkpoints it creates.

`get_state` and history reads do not call the nodes. They are suitable for an
authorized debugging page. `tasks` can provide error/interrupt information for
unfinished work. Metadata such as `source` and `step` explains how a checkpoint
was produced; it is not the application state itself.

sections.title: Example 2 — Replay tax from the previous base price
sections.body:
```python
replayed = graph.invoke(None, before_tax.config)
assert replayed["total"] == 110
```

The graph starts from the saved base and executes tax again. Our arithmetic is
deterministic, so the output is unchanged. An LLM or live currency API might give
a different output. Replaying from an already completed checkpoint does no work
because that checkpoint has no next nodes.

An external side effect downstream can also run again. A checkpoint is not an
undo log for emails, purchases, or external service changes. Use operation IDs
and safe effect design, discussed in chapter 06.

sections.title: Example 3 — Fork with a different base price
sections.body: ```python fork = graph.update_state(before_tax.config, {"base": 200}, as_node="price") result = graph.invoke(None, fork) assert result["total"] == 220 ``` `as_node="price"` says to treat this state update as an output of the price node. The runtime schedules price's successor, tax. It does not execute the price function to discover what it would return. The returned `fork` config addresses the newly created checkpoint; use that returned config when continuing. The original final checkpoint still has total 110. The lab explicitly reads it after the fork to verify that the original was preserved. Updates go through reducers, so updating an append-only list can append instead of replacing it. ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Saved base 100] --> T[Original tax: 110] P --> R[Replay tax: 110] P --> U[Update base to 200] U --> F[Fork tax: 220] ``` If parallel nodes make the last writer ambiguous, specify the intended `as_node`. Choosing a later node can skip work, so it should reflect an intentional workflow decision. Time travel can trigger human interrupts again. See the [official replay and fork guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-time-travel). **Run:** `python labs.py history`. ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python class Quote(TypedDict): base: int total: int def quote_graph(saver): g = StateGraph(Quote) g.add_node("price", lambda _: {"base": 100}) g.add_node("tax", lambda s: {"total": s["base"] * 110 // 100}) g.add_edge(START, "price").add_edge("price", "tax").add_edge("tax", END) return g.compile(checkpointer=saver) def history(): graph = quote_graph(InMemorySaver()) c = config("quote") assert graph.invoke({}, c)["total"] == 110 # 1. Inspect without executing anything. before_tax = next(s for s in graph.get_state_history(c) if s.next == ("tax",)) original_final = graph.get_state(c).config print("1. Before tax:", before_tax.values, before_tax.next) # 2. Replay reruns tax using the saved base. assert graph.invoke(None, before_tax.config)["total"] == 110 print("2. Replay total: 110.") # 3. Fork applies an update through the price node's writers. fork = graph.update_state(before_tax.config, {"base": 200}, as_node="price") assert graph.invoke(None, fork)["total"] == 220 assert graph.get_state(original_final).values["total"] == 110 print("3. Fork total: 220; original checkpoint total: 110.") ``` ```python history() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
The shared review node is in `labs.py:approval_graph`:

```python
def review(state):
    response = interrupt({"draft": state["text"], "question": "Approve or edit?"})
    return {
        "text": response.get("text", state["text"]),
        "approved": bool(response["approved"]),
    }
```

`interrupt` yields a request to the caller. With ordinary `invoke`, inspect
`result['__interrupt__']`. A later call supplies a response using
`Command(resume=...)` and the same thread ID. This is persisted waiting state,
not a Python `input()` call holding a web request open.

On resume, the interrupted node starts executing again from its beginning.
Code above `interrupt` can run again. Keep it deterministic and harmless, or
separate durable operations into appropriate tasks/nodes with idempotent effects.
Do not swallow the interrupt's control-flow exception with a broad exception
handler. See the [interrupt guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts).

sections.title: Example 1 — Approve the original draft
sections.body:
```python
paused = graph.invoke({"text": "Original draft"}, c)
assert paused["__interrupt__"]
done = graph.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": True}), c)
```

The result retains the original text and sets `approved=True`. In a real order
workflow, a conditional edge would route approved state to a fulfillment node.
The lab ends after review so it has no external side effect.

The server should authenticate the reviewer and validate the response before
passing it to the graph. The simple `bool(...)` conversion is for this controlled
lab, not validation of arbitrary HTTP JSON: for example `bool('false')` is true.
Use a Pydantic request model with strict fields in an API.

sections.title: Example 2 — Reject and end the business operation
sections.body:
```python
done = graph.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": False}), c)
assert done["approved"] is False
```

A rejection is valid data, not necessarily an exception. A real graph can route
it to a cancellation node or `END`. Do not accidentally use `if response:` on a
nonempty response dictionary; that would treat a rejection dictionary as true.
Check the actual approved field.

Store rejection reasons and reviewer identity in explicit state/audit fields if
the business process requires them. A human response should not contain arbitrary
code, database credentials, or client-selected graph routing destinations.

sections.title: Example 3 — Edit, approve and resume after a process restart
sections.body: ```python done = graph.invoke(Command(resume={ "approved": True, "text": "Human-corrected draft", }), c) ``` The edited text is returned from the review node and becomes the current state. To make the same operation survive a restart, compile with `SqliteSaver` or a service-backed saver, close the original process, reconnect, rebuild the same graph, and resume using the original thread ID. `restart_demo.py` demonstrates exactly that with three separate commands. Persisted state does not persist Python function definitions. The new process must load compatible graph code. Renaming the suspended `review` node before resuming requires a migration plan. For multiple simultaneous interrupts, inspect their returned IDs and use the supported `Command(resume={interrupt_id: response, ...})` mapping. For multiple interrupts within one node, preserve their order across restarts; do not insert or reorder interrupt calls casually. Static `interrupt_before`/`interrupt_after` breakpoints are useful for debugging and are normally continued with `None`; they do not have the same response contract as dynamic `interrupt()`. **Run:** `python labs.py interrupts`, then the three `restart_demo.py` commands from the README. ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python class Approval(TypedDict): text: str approved: bool def approval_graph(saver): def review(state): response = interrupt({"draft": state["text"], "question": "Approve or edit?"}) return {"text": response.get("text", state["text"]), "approved": bool(response["approved"])} return StateGraph(Approval).add_node("review", review).add_edge( START, "review").add_edge("review", END).compile(checkpointer=saver) def interrupts(): # Three distinct decisions, each using a different persistent thread. for n, response in enumerate([ {"approved": True}, {"approved": False}, {"approved": True, "text": "Human-corrected draft"}, ], 1): graph = approval_graph(InMemorySaver()) c = config(f"approval-{n}") paused = graph.invoke({"text": "Original draft"}, c) assert paused["__interrupt__"] assert graph.get_state(c).next == ("review",) result = graph.invoke(Command(resume=response), c) assert result["approved"] == response["approved"] assert result["text"] == response.get("text", "Original draft") print(f"{n}. Resumed:", result) ``` ```python interrupts() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Checkpoint persistence is one part of fault tolerance. It cannot atomically
commit a payment at an external service together with the graph's checkpoint
unless you explicitly design a shared transaction or coordination protocol.

sections.title: Example 1 — One parallel task succeeds while another fails
sections.body:
The `parallel_recovery` function launches `good` and `flaky` in one execution
round. Both append to a list through `operator.add`. `good` succeeds; `flaky`
raises a simulated service error on its first call.

```python
try:
    graph.invoke({"results": []}, c, durability="sync")
except RuntimeError:
    pass
result = graph.invoke(None, c, durability="sync")
```

Observed call counts are `{'good': 1, 'flaky': 2}`. The completed sibling's task
writes are available to recovery, so it need not run again. The resumed result
contains both `good` and `recovered`. This is why `put_writes` is essential in a
custom saver; a saver that only implements full-state put/get can appear to work
for a linear success case and still mishandle recovery.

This lab tests a raised exception after a successful sibling write. It does not
claim that arbitrary machine power loss can never cause repeated work. Crash
timing, durability mode, database settings, and external effects still matter.

sections.title: Example 2 — Retry a transient failure without a separate resume call
sections.body:
```python
builder.add_node(
    "transient", transient_node,
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(
        initial_interval=0.001, max_attempts=2,
        jitter=False, retry_on=ConnectionError,
    ),
)
```

The lab's first attempt raises `ConnectionError`; the second returns a result.
The invocation completes normally with count 4. The tiny delay and disabled
jitter keep the teaching test quick; real services usually need appropriate
backoff, jitter, timeouts and retry limits.

Retries repeat the failed node/task. Recovery resumes a saved execution after an
invocation failed or stopped. Both may revisit code with side effects. Retry only
errors that are reasonably transient; malformed data will not become valid
because you retry it five times.

sections.title: Example 3 — Survive the “effect succeeded, checkpoint not saved” window
sections.body: The lab simulates a payment table with a unique `operation_id`: ```sql CREATE TABLE payments ( operation_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, amount INTEGER ); ``` Two attempts to record `order-7:charge` create one row and a total of 500. The stable operation ID represents the business action, not the process attempt. Generating a new UUID on each retry defeats the protection. For a remote payment service, use its idempotency-key feature and preserve the same key on retry. For an email service with no idempotency guarantee, an outbox can coordinate your application's intent and delivery attempts, but delivery semantics still depend on the downstream receiver. Avoid promising exactly-once effects based solely on checkpoint storage. An outbox design records an operation in a business transaction, lets a worker deliver it, and records the delivery result. The graph stores the operation ID and queries its status on recovery. This keeps long-running graph logic outside an open database transaction. **Run:** `python labs.py failures`. The custom saver runs the same pending-write scenario in `python labs.py custom` and in the automated tests. ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python class Parallel(TypedDict): results: Annotated[list[str], operator.add] def parallel_recovery(saver): calls = {"good": 0, "flaky": 0} def good(_): calls["good"] += 1 return {"results": ["good"]} def flaky(_): calls["flaky"] += 1 if calls["flaky"] == 1: raise RuntimeError("Simulated service outage") return {"results": ["recovered"]} g = StateGraph(Parallel) g.add_node("good", good).add_node("flaky", flaky) g.add_edge(START, "good").add_edge(START, "flaky") g.add_edge("good", END).add_edge("flaky", END) graph = g.compile(checkpointer=saver) c = config("parallel") try: graph.invoke({"results": []}, c, durability="sync") except RuntimeError as exc: assert "Simulated" in str(exc) else: raise AssertionError("Expected the first run to fail") assert saver.get_tuple(c).pending_writes result = graph.invoke(None, c, durability="sync") assert sorted(result["results"]) == ["good", "recovered"] assert calls == {"good": 1, "flaky": 2} return calls def failures(): # 1. Pending writes prevent rerunning the successful parallel node. print("1. Recovery call counts:", parallel_recovery(InMemorySaver())) # 2. Explicit retry handles a transient error inside one invocation. attempts = [] def transient(state): attempts.append(1) if len(attempts) < 2: raise ConnectionError("Temporary") return {"count": state["count"] + 1} g = StateGraph(CounterState).add_node("transient", transient, retry_policy=RetryPolicy(initial_interval=0.001, max_attempts=2, jitter=False, retry_on=ConnectionError)) graph = g.add_edge(START, "transient").add_edge("transient", END).compile( checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) assert graph.invoke({"count": 3}, config("retry"))["count"] == 4 assert len(attempts) == 2 print("2. Transient node succeeded on attempt 2.") # 3. Simulated external payment ledger: idempotency belongs at the effect. with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as ledger: ledger.execute("CREATE TABLE payments (operation_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, amount INT)") def charge(): ledger.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO payments VALUES (?, ?)", ("order-7:charge", 500)) ledger.commit() charge() # Imagine a crash after the charge, before checkpoint commit. charge() # Retrying the same logical operation is harmless here. assert ledger.execute("SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments").fetchone()[0] == 500 print("3. Two attempts created one payment, using a stable operation ID.") ``` ```python failures() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Install `langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite`. Use `SqliteSaver` for synchronous graph
calls and `AsyncSqliteSaver` for asynchronous calls. A filesystem path persists
across processes; `':memory:'` lives only as long as its SQLite connection.

```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver
with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string("data/checkpoints.db") as saver:
    graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=saver)
    result = graph.invoke(inputs, {"configurable": {"thread_id": "chat-1"}})
```

Keep the context manager open while using the graph. The context manager returned
by `from_conn_string` is not itself the saver. The built-in SQLite saver performs
its table setup lazily. Its current layout includes `checkpoints` and `writes`;
do not assume PostgreSQL uses the same names or structure. The package's
[source and setup behavior](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/checkpoint-sqlite/langgraph/checkpoint/sqlite/__init__.py)
are useful when inspecting raw tables.

sections.title: Example 1 — Close, reconnect and read the saved count
sections.body:
In `sqlite_examples`, a file-backed saver runs count 8 to 9 and closes. A new
saver connects to the same absolute temporary path and a newly compiled graph
reads count 9 using thread `durable`.

There is no Python object shared between these savers. The state came from the
database. With `':memory:'`, the second connection would see a different empty
database. With a relative path, launching your application from another working
directory might accidentally open a different file.

For a persistent project database, create the parent directory first and resolve
the file location from application configuration. Do not depend on an arbitrary
terminal's current directory.

sections.title: Example 2 — Save an approval that another process can resume
sections.body:
The first saver runs the review graph until `interrupt`. The second saver
recompiles that graph and calls `Command(resume={'approved': True})` with the same
thread. The approval completes without rerunning the initial request as new input.

`restart_demo.py` extends this into separate operating-system processes. This
models an approval arriving tomorrow after your API service was restarted. The
database must remain on durable storage; a file inside a disposable container
without a volume will disappear when that container is replaced.

If the graph changes between those processes, verify compatibility with saved
state and pending node names before resuming old workflows.
